name: hpp-proto
workload: Deserialize, set_message, and set_message+serialize operations on the benchmarks.proto dataset from Google Protocol Buffers v3.6.0, comparing proto2/proto3 in regular and arena/non-owning modes
claimed_speedup: Deserialize (non-owning) proto2: 141ns hpp-proto vs 210ns google (~1.5x); proto3: 160ns vs 252ns (~1.6x); repeated_packed: 2624ns hpp-proto vs 4164ns google (regular). Set_message+serialize (arena/non-owning) proto2: 99.6ns vs 186ns (~1.9x); proto3: 121ns vs 223ns (~1.8x). Google is faster on serialize-only of already-built objects: 64.5ns vs 85.1ns (proto2).
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 17.0.0 (Mac); gcc 13.3.0 (Linux); Google protobuf v33.2
hardware: Apple M1 Pro (Mac); 11th Gen Intel Core i9-11950H @ 2.60GHz (Linux)
tradeoffs: Requires C++23 compiler (Clang 19+ / GCC 13+); Google protobuf still wins on pure serialize-only of already-constructed objects; biggest gains require the non-owning/arena mode, which changes ownership semantics vs stock generated protobuf classes
caveats: Only two hardware platforms tested (one Mac, one Linux box), no variance/error bars reported; result is mixed rather than a uniform win across all operations
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'HFT low latency binary serialization C++ library github faster than protobuf' surfaced huangminghuang/hpp-proto; opened repo and benchmarks/ReadMe.md via gh api

name: Microsoft Bond (Compact Binary v1)
workload: Encoded uncompressed byte size of real-world JSON documents (SchemaStore test-suite samples) re-encoded via each format's own schema; e.g. the JSON Resume example (~2.1KB source JSON) and the CircleCI-blank example (<100 bytes)
claimed_speedup: JSON Resume doc: Bond Compact Binary v1 = 2256 bytes vs FlatBuffers 3116 bytes (~28% smaller) and Cap'n Proto binary 3152 bytes / packed 2549 bytes (11-28% smaller) (derived from page data: (3116-2256)/3116). CircleCI-blank doc: Bond 10 bytes vs FlatBuffers 20 bytes vs Cap'n Proto binary 24 bytes (packed capnp is smaller at 6 bytes).
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars (microsoft/bond); open-source support ended 2025-03-31, repo archived
tradeoffs: Comparison is static wire-size only, not runtime speed; Bond is not uniformly smallest across all documents or formats (varint formats like Avro/MessagePack/Protobuf beat it on raw size, just not on FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto); the Bond project itself is discontinued
caveats: Independent third-party benchmark (jviotti/binary-json-size-benchmark, archived Nov 2023, tool versions stated: capnp 0.8.0, flatc 1.12.0, Bond C++ 9.0.4) measures encoded size only, not CPU time, so hardware/compiler flags are not applicable/stated; results vary per document — quoted numbers are for 2 of the ~24 documents in the suite, not an aggregate
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/jviotti/binary-json-size-benchmark/readme, found via WebSearch 'HFT low latency binary serialization C++ library github faster than protobuf' -> jviotti/binary-json-size-benchmark listed Microsoft Bond as an unlisted competitive format

name: Lite³ (lite3)
workload: JSON-compatible zero-copy B-tree binary format; project claims reference the simdjson Twitter API dataset (~632kB) and the Kostya JSON benchmark (~115MB) plus an unnamed comparison against Google FlatBuffers, but no runnable benchmark harness ships in this repo
claimed_speedup: outperforms the fastest SIMD JSON libraries by up to 120x; outperforms Google FlatBuffers by 242x
tradeoffs: Core library is C, not C++ (a separate C++ port, jasoncoposky/lite3-cpp, exists but has only 1 star and is unverified for the same performance); schemaless self-describing design costs ~40% extra size vs raw JSON on the cited Twitter dataset; O(log n) rather than O(1) field access
caveats: 242x and 120x figures are stated with no compiler, flags, or CPU model, and 242x is far above the 50x implausibility threshold, so evidence is capped at tier C; no /bench directory or reproducible harness exists in the repo itself — only prose claims on the docs site referencing three named external benchmark suites that are not linked from this project's own code
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "zero-copy serialization" --sort stars (top hit, updated same day)

name: psio / pSSZ (successor to fracpack)
workload: Geomean of encode/decode/validate/view latency and encoded size across multiple struct shapes (fixed records, vectors of variable elements, nested types), benchmarked against the canonical C++ libraries libprotobuf, libcapnp, libflatbuffers and msgpack-cxx
claimed_speedup: Decode geomean: pssz is 6.36x faster than protobuf, 5.38x faster than Cap'n Proto, 18.67x faster than msgpack-cxx, 1.23x faster than flatbuffers. Validate geomean: 48.01x faster than protobuf, 8.45x faster than flatbuffers, 6.12x faster than Cap'n Proto. Encode geomean: 43.40x faster than protobuf, 81.96x faster than Cap'n Proto, 57.28x faster than flatbuffers, 33.38x faster than msgpack. Protobuf/msgpack/avro instead win on raw wire size (0.56-0.65x of pssz's size).
hardware: Apple M-series (exact CPU model not specified)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; project is a 0.1.0 development/pre-release checkout
tradeoffs: No OSI license file in the repo; benchmark uses psio's own in-repo harness (first-party, not an independent third party) though it links against the real canonical libraries rather than reimplementations; fixed-width offset table design trades wire size for zero-copy random access and O(1) field lookup
caveats: First-party benchmark; hardware stated only as 'Apple M-series', not an exact CPU model, so capped below tier A despite otherwise rigorous methodology (stated compiler/flags, anchored CSV snapshot with commit hash, anti-dead-code-elimination controls); 0 GitHub stars and pre-1.0 status; fracpack itself (named in the KNOWN_LIST-adjacent search) is explicitly deprecated in favor of pssz within this same repo
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'FracPack github zero-copy serialization C++ repo' -> gofractally/psio; opened repo and docs/format-comparison.md via gh api

name: Cornflakes
workload: Custom Rust key-value store and echo server serving a CDN image-object trace (1M objects, 1KB-116MB, mean ~20KB), a Twitter cache trace, and Redis GET/MGET/LRANGE commands, over kernel-bypass 100Gb NICs
claimed_speedup: CDN trace: Cornflakes 366.5K objects/sec vs Cap'n Proto 161.0K (+128%), FlatBuffers 181.2K (+102%), Protobuf 186.1K (+97%) (Table 2). Twitter cache trace: 15.4-45.9% higher throughput than baselines at matched p99 tail latency (52-61us, Figure 7). Redis integration: 15-40.1% higher throughput on get/mget/lrange (Table 3).
hardware: 2x 24-core AMD EPYC 7402P 2.80GHz servers (CloudLab c6525-100g), Dual-port Mellanox ConnectX-5Ex 100Gb NICs, jumbo frames MTU 9000, Ubuntu 20.04 / Linux 5.04
tradeoffs: Rust-primary implementation; README states C-bindings to the serialization code exist but this was not independently verified for C++ usability; requires DPDK or Mellanox/Intel ICE NIC drivers and hugepages (kernel-bypass networking), so it is not a drop-in library without specialized datacenter NIC hardware; zero-copy only helps once field/object sizes exceed the measured ~512-byte threshold — for small objects Cornflakes only ties the baselines, it does not beat them
caveats: Baselines are the 'protobuf'/'flatbuffers'/'capnp' Rust crates wrapping each C/C++ library, not the canonical C++ implementations benchmarked directly in C++; explicit rustc compiler version/optimization flags were not located in the reviewed sections of the paper; repo last commit is Jan 2024 (stale)
